node.label: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham
node.description: Argues that race structures the meanings of gender, class and sexuality. Her 1992 intervention challenges insufficient racial analysis in feminist theory and develops an account of race as socially constructed, contested power.
node.representative_figures_and_works: African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race (1992). Further selected bibliography: Righteous Discontent: The Women’s Movement in the Black Baptist Church, 1880–1920 (1993).
node.scope_note: A theoretical contribution within Black history as well as feminist historiography. Her opening acknowledges useful feminist resources and earlier Black scholarship; it does not license an indiscriminate critique edge to every cited theorist. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham adapts Foucault’s technologies terminology to race, gender and sexuality (1992).

incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.

incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham recalls that her father’s devotion to Woodson’s historical mission led her into history, a commitment she later deepened through reading Woodson.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own oral-history testimony,16June2011, transcribed by Ashley Robertson in the2012 NPS study, printed185 and188. Albert N. D. Brooks is the essential intermediary; this does not make Woodson her personal academic supervisor. Higginbotham also identifies insufficient attention to African American women in the earlier scholars’ groundwork at188; admiration does not erase that qualification. Her father’s recollections, her childhood visits and her later reading remain distinct. Only selected transcript passages were read; no interview recording or full monograph reading is claimed.

incident_edges.relationship: Bederman credits Higginbotham’s analysis of race and gender among recent theoretical discussions informing the intersection she investigates.
incident_edges.evidence_note: At5 Bederman explicitly adopts Hazel Carby’s call to interrogate racial specificity and whiteness. Note23 also identifies Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, together with Berger/Brown/Hewitt and Lerner, as important recent theoretical discussions. This plural, bounded historiographic resource does not replace the more direct Carby credit or imply exclusive derivation. Higginbotham original unread; no guessed correction of the date as printed in Bederman’s note.

The original article remains unread; neither an editorial tribute nor a citation-chain inference supplies the relationship.

sources.citation: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, “African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race,” Signs 17, no. 2 (Winter 1992): 251–274.

verification.note: Primary opening pp. 251–252 and notes 1–2 read. Higginbotham credits feminist conceptual resources while criticizing inadequate racial analysis; the notes name Scott, Butler and earlier women-of-color scholarship. Remaining examples and later reception have not been checked in full. Addendum 2026-10-25: [Response audit: Response-edge audit, separately scoped check. Locators: Signs 17.2 (1992), p251 acknowledgment; Signs 17.2 (1992), p252 and n4; Signs 17.2 (1992), p274 and n67. Reading extents: Fresh primary acknowledgment on printed p251; no date of the feedback meeting is inferred. | Fresh primary p252 and n4; not a fresh full reading of Foucault or de Lauretis. | Fresh primary printed pp251–252 and 274 read from the institutional PDF; the remaining article was not reread. Prior verification retained. Bibliographic concordance is not whole-book reading.] Addendum 2026-10-28: Fresh public Wooster institutional PDF retrieved 200; selected actual 266/n44 and 272–273 read, 266 visually checked. 266 explicitly uses Hine’s dissemblance argument within discussion of racialized sexuality and political discourse, especially middle-class women. 272–273 also addresses repression of folk expression and silencing of AIDS/gender/class/sexual-orientation problems: this is Higginbotham’s extension/qualification of racial uplift and silence, not automatically a personal polemic against Hine. Earlier 251 draft-feedback reading preserved as a different relation/kind. Remaining examples not freshly reread and cited originals unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Kerber expressly credits Higginbotham’s interpretation of race as a resource for her discussion of Black women and the separate-spheres framework.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed26/n30 acknowledges an interpretive debt to Evelyn Brooks, The Problem of Race in Women’s History, alongside separately credited work by the Hortons, Sterling, Jones and Deborah Gray White. Higginbotham’s own Harvard CV establishes the identity through that distinctive chapter title and editor; metadata does not itself establish the debt. Kerber’s forthcoming volume title is preserved, not silently replaced with the later 1989 title. Printed9 also thanks Evelyn Brooks for counsel on earlier drafts, among many colleagues; no individual task or final chapter edition is inferred. Higginbotham chapter itself unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Hine uses Higginbotham’s account of churches as safe spaces to support her explanation of Black institutions that nurtured political discussion and resistance under segregation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Briggs 1066/n48 explicitly points to Righteous Discontent (1993), 10 for the church’s safe-space role. This particular historical resource supports Hine’s account of parallel institutions, not full adoption of every claim about respectability or proof of personal training. Kevin Gaines’s 1997 review is separately cited in the same note and is not erased. Original book/review unread; 1989 n9 earlier Burroughs chapter separately held with identity/source limits.

incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham explicitly uses Hine’s culture of dissemblance to explain Black women’s protective silence about sexuality and the political significance of their self-representation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Recipient’s own 1992 printed 266/n44 names and develops Hine’s argument, particularly for middle-class women, within a discussion of racialized sexuality and double-voiced discourse. This conceptual resource differs from existing 1622 Hine’s named draft feedback on 251. Higginbotham 272–273 also addresses costs of respectability/silencing; resource use does not mean complete agreement or that Hine originated every component of Higginbotham’s framework. Original cited Hine 1989 freshly checked; other cited scholars unread.
